instruction:
Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `parser` that implements the parser for TRI-27 assembly, turning a token stream from the lexer into an AST. Bring in the lexer and the shared `ast.t27` via `using` imports. Define a `Parser` struct holding the token slice, a position index, the current token and a `CompilerContext`, and give it a `Parser.new(tokens, source_file)` constructor that seeds an empty `Program` root with a fresh `SymbolTable` and phase set to Parsing.

Provide the usual token-cursor helpers — advance, peek, check, consume, expect, match, skip_newlines, skip_to_newline, skip_line — where consume/expect record a `CompileError` on mismatch rather than aborting. Then write the recursive-descent entry point `parse_program()` plus the productions it needs: `.const` definitions (registering a symbol), a `.data` section handling `.dword`, `.dspace` and `.dtrit` declarations, a `.code` section that collects labels and instructions, `parse_instruction()` with opcode-mnemonic lookup, and `parse_operand()` covering registers, `#immediate`, labels and `[base + offset]` memory forms.

Also support the spec-style surface: `spec` declarations, `test` blocks with given/when/then clauses, `invariant` and `rule` blocks, and the comment-driven `.test` / `.invariant` / `.bench` sections that pull name, Verify/Expected/Setup/Rationale, Measure/Target and inferred units out of `;` comments. Add a top-level `parse(source, source_file)` that tokenizes then parses, a `validate_spec()` TDD contract check, a language-policy check rejecting Cyrillic identifiers outside docs paths, and line/column helpers.

Cover it with tests for empty input, const, data, code, operand forms, each comment-driven section, spec style, opcode lookup and both language-policy cases; invariants for no-crash-on-empty, symbol-table consistency and the TDD contract; and throughput/latency benchmarks over small assembly sources.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect called `git_commands` specifying the `tri git` subcommands, which wrap git behind the Tri skill workflow from ADR-002. It imports the skill registry module.

Specify three public entry points returning i32 exit codes: `git_commit(all, message, mode)`, `git_push(remote, branch, mode)` and `git_status_with_skill()`. All of them read `.trinity/skills/registry.json`.

Commit must enforce NO-COMMIT-WITHOUT-ISSUE: refuse when the registry is missing, when there is no active or last-sealed skill, or when the skill has no bound issue, telling the user to run `tri skill begin --issue N`. A sealed skill with a TOXIC verdict is refused. Otherwise build the commit message — auto-summarise `git status` when no message was given, otherwise append `issue:<id>` if it is not already present — stage everything when `--all`, commit, then record the resulting hash back into the registry. In strict mode also append `seal:<hash>` and print a note that a push must follow.

Push must require a sealed, non-toxic skill and apply the Policy Matrix by skill kind: `recovery` needs at least 3 checkpoints plus spec and docs artifacts, `hotfix` needs at least 1 checkpoint. In strict mode the remote must be github.com/gHashTag/t27. On success update the registry with pushed status and timestamp.

Add helpers for finding the active/last-sealed skill, updating the registry, summarising status counts (modified/added/deleted, "no changes" when empty), counting checkpoints, timestamps, substring counting and int-to-string. Declare `Skill` and `SkillRegistry` structs. Finish with tests for each gate, the summariser and the checkpoint counter, invariants on exit-code sign, and latency benchmarks for the three commands.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `runtime-execute` covering task execution, promises, cancellation and timeouts.

Declare constants for a 30s default timeout, a max of 16 concurrent executions, a 100 ms poll interval and a 32-byte task id length. Model the state machines as `enum(u8)`: `ExecResultType` (success/timeout/cancelled/error), `TaskState` (pending/running/completed/failed/cancelled), `CancelReason` (user_requested/timeout/error/shutdown) and `PromiseState` (pending/resolved/rejected/cancelled).

Define `TaskID` as a fixed byte array, plus structs `Task` (id, name, command, args, env as KEY=VALUE pairs, optional cwd, timeout), `TaskResult` (task id, result type, optional exit code, stdout, stderr, duration, optional error message), `ExecContext` (task, start time, state, cancel_requested), `Promise` (task id, state, optional result, creation time, optional resolve/reject callbacks) and `ExecError`.

Specify constructors — `task_id_generate`, `task_create`, `task_with_timeout`, `result_success`/`result_timeout`/`result_cancelled`/`result_error`, `context_create`, `promise_create`, `promise_with_resolve`, `error_create` — and behaviour functions: `promise_resolve`/`promise_reject`/`promise_cancel` which move the promise state and fire the callback if present, `run`, `cancel`, `run_sync`, `run_with_timeout`, `fork`, the `is_running`/`is_pending`/`is_terminal` and `is_success`/`is_error`/`is_timeout` and `promise_is_*` predicates, `duration`, and byte/timestamp helpers.

Write Zig-style `test "..."` blocks using `std.testing.expect` for creation defaults, each result kind, context state transitions and promise resolve/reject; invariants asserting the constants are positive and the enum tag values are as declared; and latency benchmarks for task, result, promise and context creation and for duration.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `bus-schema` that defines the event types and structures for the Trinity event bus. Import `tritype-base::usize`.

Declare public constants: default channel size 1000, max payload 1048576 bytes, default subscriber buffer 100, max 100 subscribers per topic, default event TTL 60000 ms, plus the wildcard topic `"*"` and the topic separator `"/"`.

Define `enum(u8)` types with explicit tag values for `EventType` (lsp_request/response/notification, provider_request/response, the four provider_stream_* variants, system_error, system_info, custom — 0 through 11), `EventPriority` (low/normal/high/urgent), `BusState` (stopped/starting/running/stopping/error), `EventAck` and `DeliveryMode` (fire_and_forget/at_least_once/exactly_once). Add structs for `Event`, `EventFilter`, `EventResult`, `EventBatch`, `EventMetadata`, `TopicPattern`, `EventStats`, `BusConfig`, `Subscription`, `SubscriptionInfo`, `UnsubscribeResult` and `BusError`.

Specify constructor functions for each of those (`event_create` defaulting to normal priority and the default TTL, `event_with_priority`, `event_filter_create`, `event_result_create`/`event_result_error`, `topic_pattern_create` which flags the wildcard, `bus_config_default`, `subscription_create`, `subscription_info_create`, `unsubscribe_result_create`, `bus_error_create`, `event_stats_create`) plus `event_type_to_string`, `priority_to_string`, `bus_state_to_string`, `is_wildcard_pattern`, `topic_matches_pattern`, `event_matches_filter` (empty type or topic lists mean "match everything", priority must be at least the filter minimum), `is_bus_running` and `is_payload_valid`.

Cover every constructor and predicate with a `test "..."` block using `std.testing`, add invariants using `@compileAssert` that pin the enum tag ranges and the positivity of each constant, and add latency benchmarks for event creation, pattern creation, pattern matching, filter matching, the running check and type-to-string.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `TernaryDeque` specifying a fixed-capacity double-ended queue over trit values, part of Ring 088. Import `base::types`.

Use the flat, parser-friendly convention: no encapsulating struct, instead every operation takes the backing `[]i32` slice plus pointers to `front`, `back` and `count`. Declare the trit constants (-1/0/+1) and a `DEQUE_MAX_SIZE` of 27, and implement the buffer as a circular one that wraps both indices at that bound.

Specify `deque_init`, `deque_push_front`, `deque_push_back`, `deque_pop_front`, `deque_pop_back`, `deque_peek_front`, `deque_peek_back`, `deque_is_empty`, `deque_is_full`, `deque_size` and `deque_clear`. Pushes must return false when the deque is already at capacity and pops must return false when it is empty; peeks write through an out-pointer and leave the count alone; init and clear zero the backing array and reset all three indices.

Add tests for init leaving an empty deque, push_back/pop_front and push_front/pop_back round-trips, both peeks, the empty/full predicates, filling to capacity and having the next push fail, and clear. Add invariants that size equals pushes minus pops, that popping from an empty deque fails from both ends, that back-push/front-pop gives FIFO order while front-push/front-pop gives LIFO order, and that peeking does not change the size. Finish with benchmarks for push_back, push_front, pop_front, peek and a mixed workload.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `ternary_add` — Ring 043 — giving the formal treatment of balanced-ternary addition: carry propagation, closure and the range formula. Import `base::types` for `Trit`.

Specify a public `FullAdderResult` struct (sum, carry_out) and `trit_full_adder(a, b, c_in)`. The raw sum lies in [-3, +3]; normalise it into {-1, 0, +1} and emit a carry of +1 when the raw sum exceeds 1, -1 when it is below -1, and 0 otherwise — so +2 gives sum -1 carry +1, +3 gives sum 0 carry +1, and symmetrically on the negative side.

Add the capacity functions `max_value(k)` = (3^k - 1)/2, `min_value(k)` = -max_value(k) and `total_states(k)` = 3^k, computed by an explicit loop rather than a float pow. Add `trit_mul_closed(a, b)` as an exhaustive switch showing multiplication is closed over the trit domain, a `verify_trit_mul_closure()` that checks all nine products, and the two normalisation helpers `carry_sign(raw)` and `normalize_trit(raw)`.

Write tests for the interesting adder cases (both saturating directions, the zero identity, commutativity, a carry-propagation chain), for the range at k = 1, 2, 3 and 27 — including max_value(27) == 3936808944 and total_states(27) == 7625597484987 — and for every multiplication and normalisation rule. Then state the algebraic invariants with a short rationale comment each: closure, commutativity of both operations, the range formula and its symmetry, states as a power of three, sum and carry staying inside the trit domain, idempotent normalisation and the additive identity. Close with latency benchmarks for the adder, max_value(27), the multiplier and a 27-trit carry chain.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `TernaryEncoding` — Ring 065 — defining how binary data maps to ternary and back. Import `base::types`.

Declare the trit constants (-1/0/+1), encoding-scheme tags for balanced, unipolar and binary-coded ternary, and the grouping sizes: 8 bits per byte, 6 trits per byte (3^6 = 729 > 256) and 3 trits per nibble (27 > 16).

Specify the conversions: `bit_to_trit_pair` (0 becomes [0,0], 1 becomes [+1,0]); `bits_to_trits` mapping a nibble to 3 balanced trits, where a remainder of 2 is written as -1 with the quotient incremented; `trits_to_bits` inverting that by treating -1 as 2 and accumulating powers of three; `byte_to_trits`/`trits_to_byte` doing the same over a caller-supplied slice with a length, padding the tail with zeros; `char_to_trits`/`trits_to_char` as ASCII aliases; and the trivial `balanced_to_unipolar`/`unipolar_to_balanced` shifts by one.

Add validators `is_valid_trit`, `is_valid_unipolar_trit` and `validate_trits`, plus an `EncodingInfo` struct (encoding type, trits used, byte value, validity) returned by `get_encoding_info`, which only computes the byte value when the trits validate.

Write tests for both bit_to_trit_pair cases, the nibble round trip across 0..15, the byte round trip, the balanced/unipolar mapping, and both validators including out-of-range inputs, plus an ASCII round trip over a handful of characters. Add invariants for the balanced↔unipolar identity, the byte round trip across all 256 values, the nibble round trip, and that EncodingInfo reports validity and trit count correctly. Finish with benchmarks for byte-to-trits, trits-to-byte and the representation shift.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `PinsIR` that models the intermediate representation for FPGA pin assignments, I/O standards and clock constraints. Import `base::types` and `base::ops`.

Define structs `PinLocation` (package pin, port name, bank), `IoStandard` (name, voltage, drive strength in mA, fast-slew flag), `SignalReference` (port name, direction, width, index where -1 means "not indexed"), `Binding` (location, standard, signal, is_clock, pullup, pulldown), `ClockDef` (port, name, period_ns, waveform_high_ns, add flag) and a `Design` that uses fixed arrays — 256 bindings and 16 clocks — with explicit `binding_count` and `clock_count` fields rather than dynamic vectors. Provide an `LVCMOS33` constant at 3.3 V, 12 mA, slow slew.

Specify the builders `make_input_signal`, `make_output_signal`, `make_indexed_signal`, `make_location`, `make_binding` (defaulting to LVCMOS33 with no pull), `make_clock` and `empty_design`, plus `add_binding` and `add_clock` which append while respecting the array bounds.

Then specify the checks: `has_pin_conflict` (two bindings on the same non-empty package pin), `has_port_conflict` (same non-empty port name at the same index), `clock_bound` and `all_clock_ports_bound` (every binding flagged as a clock must have a matching ClockDef), plus the small accessors `binding_count`, `clock_count`, `signal_direction`, `is_indexed` and `format_port_name`.

Cover every builder and both conflict detectors with given/then tests — including a duplicate-pin conflict, two indexed `led` bits that must not conflict, and both outcomes of the clock-binding check. Add invariants that an empty design has no conflicts, is vacuously clock-bound and has non-negative counts, and benchmark `make_binding` and `has_pin_conflict`.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `RadixEconomy` giving the information-theoretic argument for base-3 computing. It uses the `Constants` module.

Pin the numbers as f64 constants: E(2) = ln(2)/2, E(3) = ln(3)/3, E(e) = 1/e, log2(3) and log3(2), each with the literal value to full double precision.

Specify `radix_economy(b)` = ln(b)/b, `efficiency_ratio(b)` relative to E(e), `base_advantage(b1, b2)` as the ratio of two economies, `info_density_bits(b)` = log2(b), and the capacity functions `ternary_range(n)` = (3^n - 1)/2 for balanced ternary and `binary_range(n)` = 2^n - 1. Because the spec must be self-contained, also specify the math helpers it leans on: `ln` via the atanh series to the ninth term, `log2` as ln(x)/ln(2), `pow` with binary exponentiation for integer exponents and a series expansion otherwise, `exp`, and `floor`.

Write tests establishing that E(3) is at least 99.5% of the optimum and at most 100%, that E(3) beats E(2) by at least 5%, that log2(3) sits in [1.58496, 1.58497] and is the reciprocal of log3(2), that 27 trits land between 2^42 and 2^43 and 18 trits between 2^28 and 2^29, and that the computed economies and logarithm helpers agree with the constants to 1e-6.

Then state the mathematical invariants — 99.5% optimality, base-3 superiority, the 5.4% advantage, the log2(3) bounds, E(b) peaking at b = e, both range formulas, the two range-equivalence claims and the log reciprocal identity — each followed by a one-line `// Rationale:` comment. Finish with cycle-count benchmarks for radix_economy, log2, ternary_range(27) and base_advantage(3, 2).

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `GF4` defining GoldenFloat4, the 4-bit phi-structured floating point format from NUMERIC-STANDARD-001. Import `numeric::goldenfloat_family` and `numeric::phi_ratio`.

The layout is [S|E|MM]: 1 sign bit, 1 exponent bit, 2 mantissa bits, exponent bias 0, and a recorded phi_distance of 0.1180339887498949 for the 1:2 exponent-to-mantissa split. Wrap the 4-bit value in a `GF4` struct with a single `raw : u4` field.

Specify `encode(f32) -> GF4` and `decode(GF4) -> f32`. Decoding reads the sign bit, the exponent bit as a scale of 1.0 or 2.0, and the 2 mantissa bits as 0, 0.25, 0.5 or 0.75, with an all-zero raw meaning zero. Encoding handles zero and negatives by recursion plus sign-bit set, and otherwise quantises to the five distinct representable positive magnitudes — 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5 — by midpoint thresholds, clamping anything above to 1.5. Add `max_value()`, `min_positive()` and `epsilon()`, a `validate_format()` that cross-checks the bit widths against the family registry, and a memory-ratio constant of 4/32.

Cover it with given/when/then tests: decoding zero, the positive maximum and a negative pattern; round-tripping each representable magnitude within 0.01; the negative and clamping cases; 0.3 quantising down to 0.25; and the format properties. Add invariants pinning each bit-width constant, the positivity and ordering of max/min/epsilon, the phi_distance bound, the encode/decode round trip over the representable set, and the sign-bit behaviour for zero, positive and negative input. Finish with nanosecond latency benchmarks for encode and decode.

Write a t27 spec, SANDBOX-012, in the module dialect for `sandbox.https_enforce`: middleware that forces HTTPS on API requests. Use a Rust-flavoured surface — byte-string literals, `&[u8]` slices, `Option`, `match`, a `trait` — and document the module and each function with `/** ... */` doc comments.

Declare the configuration: a 301 permanent-redirect status, the `https` and `http` scheme literals, and the list of local hostnames `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`. Define a public `RequestContext` struct carrying the optional `X-Forwarded-Proto` value, the host and an `is_local` flag.

Specify `should_redirect(&RequestContext) -> bool` with the rules written out in the doc comment: never redirect in local mode; do not redirect when the forwarded proto is explicitly https; redirect when it is http or the header is absent. Specify `redirect_url(&[u8]) -> Vec<u8>` which swaps an `http://` prefix for `https://` and leaves an already-https or scheme-less URL untouched, and `is_local_hostname(&[u8]) -> bool` matching against the local list. Expose a public `HttpsEnforcer` trait whose `enforce` returns `None` for no redirect and `Some(https_url)` otherwise.

Put the tests in a `.test { ... }` block, each case written as `test "name" { input: {...}; expected: ...; description: "..."; }`. Cover: https not redirected, http redirected in production, a missing proto header redirecting, localhost never redirecting, 127.0.0.1 and [::1] treated as local, a correct http-to-https rewrite, an already-https URL left alone, and a port and a query string both surviving the rewrite. Include a `make_ctx` helper in the test block that derives `is_local` from the hostname.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect for `enrichment::audio_overview` — Ring 091 — specifying bilingual (Russian and English) audio-overview generation against the NotebookLM v1alpha API.

Declare the three API endpoint path templates (create, delete-default, poll-default), the `.trinity/audio` output directory, a 30-second poll interval and a 10-minute poll timeout. Define enums `Lang` (Ru, En) and `AudioStatus` (InProgress, Completed, Failed), and structs `AudioOverviewRequest` (notebook id, language code, episode focus, optional source ids where None means all sources), `AudioOverviewResponse`, `AudioOverviewStatus`, `AudioFile` (notebook id, lang, path, duration) and `AudioReport` (processed/success/failed/skipped counts, total duration, error list).

This spec declares behaviour without bodies: give each public function a signature terminated by a semicolon, with a comment above stating the HTTP verb and endpoint or the file effect and what it returns. Cover `create_audio_overview`, `poll_audio_status`, `delete_default_audio`, `ensure_audio_dir`, `save_audio_file` (writing `.trinity/audio/{ID}/{lang}.wav`), `generate_bilingual_audio` returning the EN and RU pair, and `generate_all` as the parallel orchestrator returning an `AudioReport`.

Add tests over the builtin helpers: language-code mapping both ways, invalid codes returning the empty string, and a constructed filename containing `/ru.wav` and not `/en.wav`. Add two `forall` invariants — that language-code conversion round-trips for every code that maps, and that any audio file with content has a positive duration — and one benchmark measuring HTTP POST latency for `create_audio_overview` against a 5000 ms target.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `Storage` that defines the type vocabulary for the storage layer. Import `base::types`. Group the file into commented sections for keys, locks, migrations, errors, constants, helpers and tests.

Define `StorageKey` as a hierarchical path of string segments and `StorageEntry` as a stored value with key, value, timestamp and version. For locking, define a `LockMode` enum with explicit values Read = 0 and Write = 1, and a `Lock` struct holding the key, the mode and an acquisition timestamp. For schema evolution, define a `Migration` struct (version, name, description) and a `MigrationResult` enum (Success, Failed, Skipped).

For errors, define a base `StorageError` carrying a message and a string code, plus `NotFoundError` which also carries the missing `StorageKey` and `LockError` which carries the key and the requested mode. Add constants for a 5000 ms default lock timeout, 3 max retries and a current schema version of 2. Add the two classifier helpers `is_not_found` and `is_lock_error`, which compare the error's code against `"NOT_FOUND"` and `"LOCK_ERROR"`.

Write `test "..."` blocks with `assert(...)` covering: constructing a two-segment storage key and reading back both segments; the numeric values behind both lock modes; `is_not_found` returning true for a NOT_FOUND error and false for a PERMISSION_ERROR one; and the three constants holding their declared values. Comment each type with a one-line description of what it represents.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `compiler-mod-structure` that describes the module registry and ring validation for the Trinity spec-first architecture. It imports PHI, PHI_INV and TRINITY from `math::sacred_physics` and also restates them locally as f64 constants (1.618033988749895, 0.618033988749895, 3.0), along with a `BASE_MODULE_COUNT` of 27.

Define a public `ModuleCategory` enum with explicit values — base = 0, cloud = 1, queen = 2, compiler = 3 — and a public `ModuleEntry` struct with a name, a category, a ring number and the path to the spec file that defines it.

Specify `get_module_list()` returning a slice of `ModuleEntry`, built by appending entries in category order: the base modules `types` (ring 0, specs/base/types.t27) and `debounce` (ring 32), the cloud module `railway_deploy`, and the queen modules `consciousness`, `self_evolution` and `task_analysis`, all on ring 32 with their respective spec paths. Specify `validate_ring_number(ring) -> bool`, which accepts multiples of three (TRINITY), plus 32 and 618 as the phi-pattern exceptions.

Add a test that the module list holds at least five entries and a test that ring validation accepts 0, 3, 6 and 32. Close with an invariant named `trinity_always_holds` asserting that phi squared plus phi-inverse squared differs from TRINITY by less than 0.0001. Use doc comments (`///`) on the constants, types and functions.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `Placement_Testbench`: a testbench for the FPGA placement pass covering the placement grid, resource allocation and density constraints. It uses `fpga::placement::Placement`.

Declare the parameters as constants — a 20-unit clock period, a 50 x 40 grid, 30 CLB columns, 10 BRAM columns, 5 DSP columns and a maximum utilisation of 80 percent — and declare module-level `var` signals for clk, rst_n, place_done, utilisation and placed count, plus pass/fail counters.

Specify a `tick()` that drives the clock low then high and a `reset()` that deasserts rst_n, ticks twice, reasserts it and ticks once. Then specify the arithmetic under test: `grid_capacity()` as columns times rows; `utilization_pct(used, total)` as integer percent, returning 0 when total is zero; `check_utilization` comparing that against the 80 percent cap; and `estimate_wirelength` as the Manhattan distance between two grid positions, computed with branches rather than a signed subtraction.

Write `test name { ... }` blocks that call the functions and assert with an `invariant` line inside the block: reset leaves place_done false, capacity is 2000, 1000/2000 is 50 percent and 2000/2000 is 100 percent, 1000/2000 passes the utilisation check while 1800/2000 fails, the wirelength from (0,0) to (10,20) is 30, and the three resource column counts fit inside the grid width. Add two module-level `invariant name : expr;` declarations for positive grid dimensions and a utilisation cap of at most 100. Finish with a `bench` block that loops 100 iterations of wirelength and utilisation calls.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `MetaCompilation` that models the result of compiling a t27 spec through every backend. It uses `compiler::parser` and `compiler::lexer`.

Define a `CompileResult` struct with a parse-success flag, one success flag per backend — zig, verilog, c and rust — and a line count per backend. Add a `SAMPLE_SPEC` string constant holding a minimal one-line t27 module with an `add` function, so the spec carries its own example input.

Specify four functions over that struct: `compile_result_init()` returning a zeroed result with every flag false and every line count 0; `is_full_success(r)` requiring the parse and all four backends to have succeeded; `total_lines(r)` summing the four counts; and `any_backend_ok(r)` as the disjunction of the four backend flags.

Write the tests in the `test name / given / then` form, one per function, all starting from `compile_result_init()`: that the initial parse flag is false, that a fresh result is not a full success, that its total line count is zero, and that no backend is reported as ok. Then add two `invariant name / given / assert` declarations: that the total line count is never negative, and that a freshly initialised result is never a full success. Keep the whole spec free of I/O — it describes the shape and the algebra of the result, not the act of compiling.

Write a small t27 spec in the module dialect named `base-ring-32` that declares the Ring 32 definition for the Trinity ring registry. Import PHI, PHI_INV and TRINITY from `math::sacred_physics`.

Export three public constants: `RING_NUMBER` as a u8 equal to 32, `RING_CAPABILITY` as the string "Cloud Orchestration", and `RING_32_SPECS` as a fixed `[4]str` array naming the four spec files that belong to this ring — the railway deploy spec under specs/cloud, the debounce spec under specs/base, the queen task-analysis spec, and the compiler mod_structure spec.

Add one `test "ring_number_is_32"` asserting the ring number, and one `invariant "ring_32_has_4_specs"` asserting that the array length matches the declared array size of four, so that adding a fifth path without widening the array is caught. Keep the file short: the point of a ring definition is that it is a declaration the rest of the build can read, not an implementation. Head it with the Apache-2.0 SPDX line and the project's phi banner comment.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `forward_pass` specifying a transformer-style forward pass built entirely out of Vector Symbolic Architecture operations. Import `numeric::gf16`, `Trit` from `tritype-base`, and bind, unbind, bundle2, bundle3, permute and cosine_similarity from `vsa::vsa_core`.

Fix the shape with constants: a 1024-dimensional hypervector, 11 role vectors, a context window of 8, 3 attention heads with Q/K/V each, the last two roles being FF1 and FF2, a 100-token generation cap, a 0.5 learning rate, 5 resonator iterations and a 0.5 similarity threshold. Declare `Hypervector` as an array of Trit, `Roles` and `Context` as arrays of those, and a `TrainResult` struct with loss, similarity and iteration count.

Specify: `init_roles(dim, seed)` deterministically seeded; `single_head_attention` which binds the last position with the Q role, scores every context position's K binding by cosine similarity and returns the V binding of the best match; `forward_pass_multi_head` which permutes each context slot by its index, runs three heads, merges them with bundle3, applies the two FF binds and adds a residual by bundling with the last positioned vector; `summarize_context` as positional permute plus sequential bundling; and `forward_pass_direct` as a single bind of the summary with a role. Add `resonator_train_step`, which unbinds the target to derive ideal FF1/FF2 directions, applies them, keeps the best loss and stops early once similarity passes the threshold; `compute_direct_role`, the one-shot bundled alternative; `generate_autoregressive` with a shifting context; and `measure_perplexity` and `compute_accuracy` over a dataset.

Cover every function with `test "..."` blocks, including the empty-corpus and empty-dataset edge cases, bind/unbind self-inversion, permutation changing a hypervector, and order sensitivity of the context summary. Add invariants that dimensions are preserved by every VSA operation and that loss, similarity, accuracy and perplexity stay in their valid ranges, plus benchmarks for each operation.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `VM` describing the VSA VM — a ternary virtual machine for hyperdimensional computing. Import `base::types`, `numeric::gf16`, `vsa::vsa_core` and `ternary::hybrid_arithmetic`, and reference those specs rather than duplicating their definitions.

Define a public `VSAOpcode` enum(u8) grouped by purpose: vector ops (v_load, v_store, v_const, v_random), VSA ops (v_bind, v_unbind, v_bundle2, v_bundle3), similarity ops (v_dot, v_cosine, v_hamming), arithmetic (v_add, v_neg, v_mul), control (v_mov, v_pack, v_unpack, v_cmp), permutation (v_permute, v_ipermute, v_seq) and nop/halt. Define `VSARegisters` with four HybridBigInt vector registers v0-v3, two i64 scalars s0 and s1, four gf16 float registers f0-f3, a u32 program counter and three condition-code flags; `VSAInstruction` with opcode, dst, src1, src2 and an i64 immediate; and `VSAVM` holding the registers, a halted flag, a cycle count and a JIT-enabled flag.

Add the `vm_get_vreg`/`vm_set_vreg` helpers, where an out-of-range index reads back a zero vector and writes are ignored.

Write given/when/then tests for creation defaults, halt, nop cycle counting, mov, add, neg, dot, permute, bind and the bind-then-unbind pair, and both register accessors including the invalid index. Add invariants for cycle counting, the halted flag, zero-initialised registers and the accessor range, and benchmark create plus each instruction class.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `triformat-int4` defining a saturating 4-bit signed integer type. Declare the constants: 4 bits, a range of [-8, 7], 16 states and a 0x0F lower-nibble mask, and alias `Int4` to i8 with only the low four bits meaningful.

Every operation saturates rather than wrapping. Specify the conversions in — `int4_from_i8`, `int4_from_i16`, `int4_from_i32`, and `int4_from_f32` which rounds to nearest before clamping and maps NaN to zero — and the conversions out: `int4_to_i8` as identity, `int4_to_i16` and `int4_to_i32` with sign extension, and `int4_to_f32`/`int4_to_f64`. Specify the arithmetic `int4_add`, `int4_sub`, `int4_mul` and `int4_div`, all clamping to the range, with division by zero returning MAX or MIN according to the sign of the numerator, plus `int4_abs` and `int4_neg` which must saturate on -8. Add the comparisons `int4_is_equal`, `int4_is_greater`, `int4_is_less`, `int4_min`, `int4_max` and `int4_clamp`, and the utilities `int4_clamp_to_range`, `int4_is_in_range`, `int4_lerp`, `int4_sq` and `int4_abs_diff`.

Write Zig-style `test "..."` blocks that exercise each function at its boundaries: in-range, above max, below min and exactly at both endpoints for every conversion; overflow and underflow for add, sub and mul; both division-by-zero signs; abs and neg of MIN; and the three lerp positions. Then add invariants pinning the constants, the saturation behaviour at both ends, the additive and multiplicative identities, abs being non-negative, double negation, min/max ordering and clamp staying in range. Finish with latency benchmarks for the conversions and the three cheapest arithmetic ops.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `triformat-gf128` specifying encode and decode for GoldenFloat128: a 128-bit format laid out as 1 sign bit at 127, a 28-bit exponent at 99, and a 99-bit mantissa at 0.

Declare the shift, mask and width constants, an exponent maximum of 0x0FFFFFFF, a bias of 134217727 (2^27 - 1), an all-ones special exponent for Inf/NaN, and a phi-optimised rounding bias. Because 128-bit constants are awkward, express the masks as u64 hi/lo pairs and define a `GF128Parts` struct so a value can be split into and rebuilt from two u64 words via `gf128_to_parts` and `gf128_from_parts`.

Specify the field accessors `gf128_extract_sign`, `gf128_extract_exponent` and `gf128_extract_mantissa`, the packer `gf128_from_components`, and the named constants for positive and negative zero, both infinities and NaN, together with the classifiers `gf128_is_zero`, `gf128_is_special`, `gf128_is_inf` and `gf128_is_nan`. Specify `gf128_encode_f64` and `gf128_decode_f64`, which bridge through the f64 bit pattern with the mantissa shifted 47 bits (52 + 47 = 99), plus the f128 wrappers. Add the arithmetic `gf128_add`, `gf128_sub`, `gf128_mul` and `gf128_div` (division by zero yielding the correctly signed infinity), the sign manipulators `gf128_abs` and `gf128_neg`, and the comparisons `gf128_is_equal` (NaN never equal), `gf128_is_greater`, `gf128_max`, `gf128_min` and `gf128_clamp`.

Cover sign extraction, exponent extraction, both zeros, infinity, NaN, encode of 0, 1 and -1, an encode/decode round trip, simple add and mul, abs, neg and a from_components round trip with `test "..."` blocks. Add invariants that the three field widths sum to 128, that the bias is 2^27 - 1, that the special exponent is all ones, that positive zero has no sign bit while negative zero does, and that abs clears and neg toggles the sign. Benchmark sign extraction, encode, decode and add.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `GF256` defining GoldenFloat256, the 256-bit member of the phi-structured float family (NUMERIC-STANDARD-001). Import `numeric::goldenfloat_family` and `numeric::phi_ratio`.

The layout is 1 sign bit, 97 exponent bits and 158 mantissa bits, with the exponent bias held as a hi/lo u64 pair and a recorded phi_distance of 0.00412087369321891 — the 97/158 ratio sits within 0.005 of 1/phi. Represent the value as a `GF256` struct of four u64 words, raw_0 through raw_3, and document in comments which bit range each word covers.

Specify `encode(f64) -> GF256` and `decode(GF256) -> f64`: encoding extracts the unbiased exponent, clamps it against the 97-bit field, normalises the mantissa into 158 bits and packs sign, exponent and mantissa across the four words; decoding reverses that, treating an all-zero exponent and mantissa as zero and handling the subnormal case separately. Add `max_value()`, `min_positive()` and `epsilon()` derived from the mantissa width, a `validate_format()` cross-checking the widths against the family registry, a memory ratio of 8x FP32, and the self-contained math helpers this needs: `floor_log2`, `pow` with binary exponentiation for integer exponents, `ln_approx`, `exp_approx` and `floor`.

Write given/when/then tests for decoding an all-zero value, a zero round trip, the bit widths summing to 256, positivity of max, min_positive and epsilon, the phi_distance being under 0.01, the memory ratio, and format validation. Add invariants pinning each width constant, ordering max above min_positive, bounding the phi distance, checking the exponent/mantissa ratio against 0.618 within 0.01, and asserting the mantissa exceeds 100 bits. Finish with encode and decode latency benchmarks.

Write a t27 spec in the module dialect named `Partition` that specifies automatic partitioning of HIR modules across multiple FPGAs, including inter-FPGA bandwidth estimation. Use the flat array plus explicit count-field convention throughout so the parser can handle it.

Define `FpgaNode` (name, device, LUTs, FFs, BRAM18, DSP48, IO pins) with a generic `fpga_node` builder and an `arty_a7_node` preset for the xc7a100t: 63400 LUTs, 126800 FFs, 135 BRAM18, 240 DSP48, 300 IO. Two parser constraints must be honoured, and say so in comments: the assignment builder's first parameter is named `mod_name`, not `module`, because `module` is the keyword that opens a declaration and using it as a parameter silently drops the rest of the body; and `total_link_bandwidth` takes `[]const InterFpgaLink`, because a mutable slice parameter cannot be called from a test. That function sums only the first `count` links, not the whole array. Add `fpga_util` (integer percent, guarded against a zero-LUT node), `fpga_remaining` (clamped at zero) and `validate_node`, which counts every fault rather than returning on the first.

Write given/then tests for each builder and derived value, then the edge cases that pin the contracts: a short and a zero count truncating the bandwidth sum, both utilisation endpoints, a zero-LUT node, an exactly-full node, used plus remaining equalling capacity, both faults counted, and the SERDES/LVDS protocol tags differing. Add invariants for non-negative bandwidth and the zero-utilisation base case, and benchmark utilisation and bandwidth.

Write lesson 1 of the t27 tutorial as a spec in the module dialect, named `tutorial-01-values`. Its subject is values and types, and its thesis — state it in the header comment — is that every constant carries an explicit width because a spec has to say what reaches hardware rather than let a compiler infer it. Nothing in the file is inferred.

The file is teaching material, so the prose in the section comments matters as much as the declarations. Organise it into commented sections and give each a short explanation before the constants that illustrate it.

Cover, in order: integers, where width and signedness are part of the type name (u for unsigned, i for signed, the number being the bit width) — show u8, i8, u16, u32 and i32 constants at or near their extremes; other bases, explaining that hex and binary are ordinary integer literals and that binary is worth using when the value is a bit pattern, since a mask written as 0b111111111 documents its own width where 511 does not; floats and booleans, with an f32, an f64 and both boolean values; and the trit, explaining that this language is built on three states rather than two, that a trit lives in an i8 and is only ever -1, 0 or +1, and declaring the three trit constants plus TRINITY = 3.

Close with an invariants section explaining that an invariant states something that must hold for the module as a whole and is checked rather than decorative, then declare two: that the trit range spans exactly TRINITY states, and that the mantissa mask equals 511.
